In this case, a Detailed Accident Report (hereinafter referred as DAR) was filed by police official concerned and in terms of provisions of Motor Vehicle Act, same is treated as Claim Petition under Section 166 (1) read with Section 166 (4) MV Act. It pertains to alleged accident of injured Adhe (hereinafter referred as claimant), by offending vehicle bearing Reg. No. DL 8C AH 5757, driven by Shankar Yadav (hereinafter referred as R-1), owned by Gurucharan Singh, (hereinafter referred as R-2) and insured with United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (hereinafter referred as R-3). 
2. Preliminary information regarding accident in question was received at Police Post Sriniwaspuri,
vide DD no. 2 PP on 09.01.2020. It was informed that a truck ran over people who were sleeping on the footpath of Modi Mill Flyover, Okhla, Phase-III. It was further informed that a person had stuck in the wheels and 2-3 persons had been rescued. Thereafter, police officials reached the spot of accident and found a truck in accidental condition which ran over footpath after breaking the grill. A man was found crushed under the wheels of MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors.
Page No. 2 of 25 the Truck. Police officials also found a car bearing Reg No. DL 8C AH 5757 in accidental condition. However, they neither found driver of offending truck nor any eye witness to the accident. Crime team reached and inspected the spot. It came to light that three injured persons have already been shifted to hospital for treatment. After enquiry, the driver of aforesaid car stated that the accident had already occurred when he happened to hit the said Truck/ Trolla as he could not spot it due to darkness. The deceased / victim, under the wheel, whose name was disclosed as Lalan, was removed to AIIMS Trauma Center. Thereafter, police official reached AIIMS Trauma Center and received MLC of three injured persons namely Banpatia, Aadi and Vikas. Since they were medically opined to be unfit, their statement could not be recorded in the hospital. FIR was registered on the basis of DD entry under Section 279/337/304A IPC. Statement of injured persons were later recorded by IO wherein they narrated about details of accident. They stated that all of them including deceased have been living and begging at the spot of accident for past few days. They stated that the offending Truck Traulla bearing No. HR 38R 6325 ran over them when they were sleeping under the Modi Mill Flyover Footpath on 09.01.2020 at about 12.30 AM due to which three persons sustained injuries and another pavement dweller was crushed under the wheel. The truck driver fled from the spot after the accident. During investigation, accidental truck was seized from the spot and mechanically inspected. 
3. Notice under Section 133 MV Act served to driver and owner of the offending vehicle, seizure memo prepared. Driver of offending vehicle was arrested. Offending vehicle was taken into possession and was got mechanically inspected. Upon completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed under Sections 279/337/338/304A IPC before concerned MM. DAR was filed by MACT No.

2 4. In response to notice, R-1/ driver and R-2 /owner appeared before the Court at initial stage,
however, they chose not to file any reply/ WS despite opportunity. 
5. R-3/Insurance Company, however, filed its reply. It is stated that injured persons contributed to the negligence as they were allegedly at spot not meant for that and thus suffered on account of their own negligence. It is requested that deduction towards contributory negligence ought to be made in this matter. It is however admitted by Insurance Company that there is no statutory defence in this case. 
Issues:
6. From the pleadings of parties, following issues were framed vide order dated 13.05.2022:
1) Whether the injured suffered injury in a road traffic accident on 19.01.2020 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. HR 38R 6325 being driven by R-1, owned by R-2 and insured with R-3? OPP. 
2) Whether the petitioners are entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom ? OPP.

7. Thereafter, matter was listed before Ld. Local Commissioner for recording of evidence. Such Ld.
Local Commissioner sent its report vide order dated 26.08.2023.
8. Claimant Adhe stepped in the witness box before Ld. LC as PW-1 and tendered his examination in chief by way of affidavit as Ex.PW1/A. He relied MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav &
Ors. Page No. 4 of 25 upon following documents:
i) Copy of Aadhar Card as Ex.PW1/1 (OSR)
ii) Original Treatment Record of PW-1 as Ex.PW1/2.
(iii) Original bills as Ex.PW1/3 (colly). 
(iv) Copy of MLC as Mark -4. 
(v) Copy of DAR (in connected case titled as Arti Vs. Shankar) as 9. He was cross examined by counsel for Insurance Company.

3 11. Final Arguments in detail were addressed by Ld. Counsel for the claimants as well as Ld. Counsel for insurance company. It is argued by Ld. Counsel for Insurance Company that footpath is not meant for sleeping thus the victims had actively contributed to the accident which has been squarely contested by counsel for claimant who argued that it is the duty of the State to ensure safe shelter places to all its citizens and that nobody by its free will would opt without any compulsion to sleep on the pavement and put his life on risk. Further, that the offending vehicle was supposed to move on the road rather it crashed through the grill on the pavement which itself shows the extent of recklessness of the part of driver of the offending vehicle. Written Submissions/ computation filed on behalf of claimant as well as insurance company . 
12. On the basis of material on record, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under :-
MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 5 of 25 ISSUE NO.1 1) Whether the injured suffered injury in a road traffic accident on 19.01.2020 due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle no. HR 38R 6325 being driven by R-1, owned by R-2 and insured with R-3? OPP. 
13. It is well settled that the proceedings before the Claims Tribunal are in the nature of inquiry and the finding of rash and negligent driving by driver of the offending vehicle is to be returned only at the touch stone of preponderance of probabilities. The factors noted above are sufficient to conclude that preponderance of probability is made out showing negligence of respondent no.1 in causing the accident. 
14. Police after investigation had filed charge-sheet against respondent no.1 under Section 279/337/338/304A IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent no.1 in causing the accident. The IO has filed Detailed Accident Report before this Tribunal. In National Insurance Co.
Vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of chargesheet under relevant section are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
15. It is also settled that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box, an adverse inference can be drawn against him as observed by Hon'ble High Court of India in the case of Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310.
16. These are four connected matters. Three persons were injured in the accident while one person namely Lallan died. Three persons who are injured are called Adhe, his wife Banpatiya and his minor son Vikas. Adhe and Banpatiya were produced as petitioners witnesses in connected 3 matters being MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 6 of 25 injured persons. But in death case of Lallan, they were not produced as eye witness, however, it is not mentioned by the counsel that the testimony of injured persons be read in the death case as well being connected case pertaining to same accident. However, as these 4 DARs are the result of the same accident and the injured persons have testified about the same in their own DAR matters,
Adhe (Dar) vs Shankar Yadav(08/20, Ac) on 30 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/41404110/
4 there is no reason why those testimonies should not be read as testimonies of eye witnesses in death matter of Lallan. Therefore, evidence of Adhe and Banpatiya with respect to the mode and manner of accident as eye witness to the accident being injured themselves is being read as part and parcel of this case of death of Lallan. 
17. It is categorically testified that those three injured persons along with Lallan were resting on the footpath under the Modi Mill Flyover on 09.01.2020 when suddenly at about 12.30 AM, speeding offending vehicle crashed through the grill of the footpath and ran over them due to which Lallan was crushed under the wheels of the Truck while other three were severally injured and were rushed to the hospital for treatment. Aadhe and Banpatiya were cross examined by counsel for the insurance company in the other three matters wherein they called themselves as eye witness and as victims to the incident. They also stated during cross examination that a car had also subsequently hit the truck from behind after the accident. They also categorically attributed the entire negligence on the part of speeding offending vehicle. 
18. FIR was registered and police recorded statement of other injured persons. There are certain photographs filed on record as part of DAR which are Ex.PW1/6 to Ex.PW1/11, which are self evident of the reckless driving on the part of driver of the offending vehicle. There is no dispute with respect to the identification of the offending vehicle or that of the driver of the offending MACT No.
883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 7 of 25 vehicle. Offending vehicle was found at the spot by police whereas the charge sheet shows that the driver had fled away from the spot and his identity was subsequently revealed by the owner when notice under Section 133 MV Act was served upon him. PW-1 wife of the deceased, during cross examination by counsel for Insurance Company deposed that other three injured persons were her relatives and on the day of accident,
they came to meet her deceased husband and at the time of accident, they were sleeping along with her husband Lallan on the pavement where incident happened. R-1 & 2 has chosen not to cross examine this witness. All the injured persons have been consistent in their statement before the police as well as their testimonies before the court with respect to the details of the accident. Despite detailed cross examination by counsel for insurance company, any contradiction or inconsistency could not be elicited from the testimony of the eye witnesses. The testimony has been very natural and convincing and thus inspires confidence. There is thus no reason with the court to doubt the credibility or reliability of the witness. No witness has been produced on behalf of respondent to place any defence or to raise doubt over the veracity of the witness or the testimony itself. The offending vehicle was being driven on a public way. As such, rashness and negligence has not been defined in MACT but it entails its meaning from Sec. 279 IPC which penalises rash and negligent driving on a public way so as to endanger human life. Rashness and negligence has to be understood in a contextual sense depending upon the facts of any case. In simple terms, it would mean driving without due and reasonable care towards the traffic rules and towards the safety of fellow commuters plying on the said public way. High speed without doubt is a testament to rash driving but is not the sole exclusive criteria to so determine. In the instant case, it is evident from bare perusal of the Site Plan that the MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 8 of 25 offending vehicle could not negotiate the turn under the Modi Mill Flyover on account of its high speed and therefore, went beyond the control of the driver to breach the road and crashed into and over the footpath crushing and injuring the pavement dwellers. Such was the impact of the accident Adhe (Dar) vs Shankar Yadav(08/20, Ac) on 30 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/41404110/
5 that a crane had to be called for removing wheels of the truck from the body of deceased Lallan. The driver simply fled away from the spot without even caring to remove the wheels of the truck from the body of the person crushed under the wheels, what to talk of offering any help to the injured persons. There is no other conclusion possible than the reckless and brazen driving on the part of driver of offending vehicle was responsible for killing one and causing injuries to three others. 
Contributory negligence 19. It is argued by Ld. Counsel for insurance company that the victims contributed to the accident by sleeping on the road pavements and therefore, contributory negligence on their part must be deducted from the compensation to be awarded to the victims. 
20. It is admitted that all the four victims were resting/ sleeping on the pavement while Lallan used to reside their in a juggi, other three had come from native village to pay him a visit. However, this Court cannot comment on the reason why those people were compelled to spend their nights on the pavement and why they could not afford to have some other suitable safe place to live. It can least be called to be unfortunate that they were compelled to be out in open on a presumably chilly January night in the National Capital. Least this Court can do is not to punish them for their helplessness which primarily made them victim of this extremely unfortunate incident. No doubt a duty of reasonable care is inherent in every living being but their might be overwhelming compulsions pushing the person to compromise on the said duty in a bare bid to MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs.
Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 9 of 25 survive. The victim must not be doubly punished for what they had to go through or what they had to lose in the accident. 
21. Therefore, the contention of Ld. Counsel for Insurance Company is rejected and this Tribunal does not hold that victim in any manner was guilty of contributory negligence. 
22. As such, in view of the evidence proved on record and charge-sheet against R-1 and that R-1 did not appear in the witness box to deny the rash and negligence on the part of driver, in backdrop of the discussion made above, nothing remains in contention any further. The contention of contributory negligence raised by counsel for insurance company stand rejected in terms of discussion made above. It is held that rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle was responsible for causing death of Lallan and injuries to the other three. Issue No.1 is decided accordingly, in favour of the petitioner and against respondent. 
ISSUE NO.2 2) Whether the claimant is entitled to any compensation, if so, to what extent and from whom ? 
OPP.
23. Section 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. Same is reproduced hereunder for ready reference:

Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 10 of 25 being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be, each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be:
Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X. (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award. (3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal,
deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct." 
24. Before putting in frame the position of law, it is noted that the process of determining the compensation by the court is essentially a very difficult task and can never be an exact science. 
Perfect compensation is hardly possible, more so in claims of injury and disability. (As observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Company Ltd, SLP (Civil) No. 19277 of 2019). 
25. The basic principle in assessing motor vehicle compensation claims, is to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in before the accident, MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 11 of 25 with other compensatory directions for loss of amenities and other payments. These general principles have been stated and reiterated in several decisions. [Support drawn from Govind Yadav v. New India Insurance Co. Ltd., (2011) 10 SCC 683] . 
26. This Tribunal has been tasked with determination of just compensation. The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC v. Mahadeva Shetty and Another,
(2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15): 
"Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just. What would be "just"
Adhe (Dar) vs Shankar Yadav(08/20, Ac) on 30 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/41404110/
7 compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal, the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims,
wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 
27. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control ( India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following observations: 
"9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 12 of 25 pecuniary damages and special damages. Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non- pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial;
(iii) other material loss. So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life." 
28. Certain principles for delineating just compensation were enumerated in the case of Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr., (2011) 1 SCC 343, by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India. Following observations are relevant in the context: 
"40.General principles relating to compensation in injury cases 5. The provision of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. 
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to Adhe (Dar) vs Shankar Yadav(08/20, Ac) on 30 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/41404110/
8 be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which MACT No.
883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 13 of 25 he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 :
1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 :
(1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .]
6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages) 
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii)(a) and (iv).
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
7. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs.
Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 14 of 25 Item (ii)(a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve Adhe (Dar) vs Shankar Yadav(08/20, Ac) on 30 January, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/41404110/
9 reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of lump sum amounts with reference to circumstances such as age, nature of injury/deprivation/ disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of this Court and the High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 
What usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii)(a). We are concerned with that assessment in this case." 
29. It is settled proposition of law as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident. Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive, and the victims who have to face their lives. 
30. It is deposed by claimant that he was doing his own work as street vendor and earning Rs.
20,000/- per month. As such, he has relied upon his Aadhar Card Ex.PW1/1 and has also admitted his permanent address to be one which is mentioned in the Aadhar Card. There is nothing to infer that he was a resident of Delhi. There is no mention in the affidavit Ex.PW1/A as to since how long were they dwelling on the footpath where accident happened. There is nothing mention in the affidavit to understand that he was residing or working in Delhi to earn his living. It is noted that he along with his wife and minor child all were MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors.
Page No. 15 of 25 permanent resident of Uttar Pradesh and have not placed any document to support the contention that they resided or worked to earn their living in Delhi. There is not even a bare affirmation in their respective testimonies to that effect. It was clarified by wife of deceased Lallan in her testimony in the connected matter that they had visited Lallan to meet him as relatives and were resting along with him when the tragedy happened. Therefore, it is accepted that Adhe along with his wife Banpatia and minor son Vikas were resident of UP on the date of accident and used to reside their and worked to earn living in UP. There is nothing mention about their formal minimum qualification of Banpatia or Adhe. Both Adhe and Banpatia testified in their respective evidentiary affidavit that they worked as street vendor and earn Rs. 20,000/- per month but there is nothing to support the bare assertion. There is no proof filed to infer the actual amount of monthly amount of injured Adhe and Banpatia. It is thus held that they used to engage as unskilled labour in Uttar Pradesh on the date of accident and their monthly income is assessed as per minimum wages applicable in the State of Uttar Pradesh as per rates notified which is Rs. 8,278/- per month. The contention of counsel for Insurance Company that Adhe Banpatiya were pavement dwellers in Delhi and used to make their living as beggars in Delhi and therefore, only notional income must be applied as they did not suffer any loss of income deserves to be rejected. 
31. As such, rashness and negligence has not been defined in MACT but it entails its meaning from Sec. 279 IPC which penalises rash and negligent driving on a public way so as to endanger human life.
Rashness and negligence has to be understood in a contextual sense depending upon the facts of any case.
In simple terms, it would mean driving without due and reasonable care towards the traffic rules and towards the safety of fellow commuters plying on the said public way.

Even as per the guidelines issued by this Court Court, long term fixed deposit of amount of compensation is mandatory only in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows.
In the case of illiterate claimants, the Tribunal is allowed to consider the request for lumpsum payment for effecting purchase of any movable property such as agricultural implements, rickshaws etc. to earn a living.
However, in such cases, the Tribunal shall make sure that the amount is actually spent for the purpose and the demand is not a ruse to withdraw money.
In the case of semi- illiterate claimants,
the Tribunal should ordinarily invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.
But if the MACT No. 883/2021 Adhe Vs. Shankar Yadav & Ors. Page No. 21 of 25 Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid.
In the case of literate persons, it is not mandatory to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

The expression used in guideline No. (iv) issued by this Court is that in the case of literate persons also the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No. (i), whereas in the guideline Nos. (i), (ii), (iii) and (v), the expression used is that the Tribunal should.
Moreover, in the case of literate persons, the Tribunal may resort to the procedure indicated in guideline No.
(i) only if, having regard to the age, fiscal background and strata of the society to which the claimant belongs and such other considerations, the Tribunal thinks that in the larger interest of the claimant and with a view to ensure the safety of the compensation awarded, it is necessary to invest the amount of compensation in long term fixed deposit.

Thus, sufficient discretion has been given to the Tribunal not to insist on investment of the compensation amount in long term fixed deposit and to release even the whole amount in the case of literate persons.
However, the Tribunals are often taking a very rigid stand and are mechanically ordering in almost all cases that the amount of compensation shall be invested in long term fixed deposit.
They are taking such a rigid and mechanical approach without understanding and appreciating the distinction drawn by this Court in the case of minors, illiterate claimants and widows and in the case of semi literate and literate persons.
The guidelines were not to be understood to mean that the Tribunals were to take a rigid stand while considering an application seeking release of the money.
